title: US Holiday cheer, at a higher price
gist: Oxford Economics forecasts US holiday retail sales up 4.2% nominal but only 2.2% real — below a typical season — as high inflation, diesel costs and Fed rate hikes squeeze most households while an equity-driven wealth effect props up high-income spending in a bifurcated consumer.

insights.claim: Oxford Economics forecasts US holiday retail sales to rise 4.2% in dollar terms and 2.2% in volume after inflation, beating last year's tariff-hit, front-loaded season but trailing a typical holiday season because of higher energy prices.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: The gap between 4.2% nominal and 2.2% real growth implies roughly 2% price growth and soft volumes; temper retail volume expectations.
insights.quote: We forecast holiday retail sales to rise 4.2% in dollar terms and 2.2% in volume after adjusting for inflation.

insights.claim: High inflation is holding down real disposable income growth, high diesel prices are raising shipping costs, and Federal Reserve rate hikes are raising borrowing costs for credit-card-funded holiday spending.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Three simultaneous squeezes — prices, freight, credit — hit lower- and middle-income consumers and retailer margins.

insights.claim: High-income consumers will keep a floor under holiday spending thanks to the surge in equities this year, with recreational goods and services, household furniture and clothing likely to benefit most from the positive wealth effect.
insights.speaker: Emma Pollard
insights.so_what: Consumer strength is a function of equity prices; favor retailers and categories skewed to affluent shoppers, and treat an equity drawdown as a spending risk.
insights.locator: This holiday season will remain deeply bifurcated
